column1: How do you justify Big-O out loud in an interview instead of just naming the formula?
column2: Explain the reason: "this is O(n) because I traverse the array only once, with no nested loop."

column1: What's the complexity difference between brute force and hash map for Two Sum?
column2: Brute force is O(n²) comparing every pair. Hash map solves it in O(n) by storing seen values for O(1) lookup.

column1: When should you use Two Pointers?
column2: On sorted arrays/strings, with pointers at both ends or moving in the same direction (e.g. removing duplicates in-place).

column1: When does Sliding Window replace a nested O(n²) loop?
column2: When the problem asks about a contiguous subarray/substring (e.g. longest substring without repetition) — the window slides instead of restarting from scratch at each position.

column1: What's the difference between a fixed-size and variable-size Sliding Window?
column2: Fixed: size never changes (e.g. moving average of k elements). Variable: grows/shrinks based on a condition (e.g. substring without repetition).

column1: What is the base case in a recursive function?
column2: The condition that stops the recursion, preventing infinite calls — it's the "when to stop."

column1: What's the risk of very deep recursion without optimization?
column2: Stack overflow — each recursive call pushes a new execution frame onto the call stack.

column1: What's the practical difference between a problem solved with simple recursion and one solved with DP?
column2: DP kicks in when there are repeated subproblems that can be cached (memoized) to avoid recomputation.

column1: Why is narrating your reasoning out loud part of what's evaluated in a live coding interview?
column2: Because communicating your plan before/during solving shows your thought process, not just the final code result.

column1: What's a good step order when solving a new LeetCode problem live?
column2: 1) Understand and restate the problem in your own words. 2) Think of examples/edge cases. 3) Verbalize your approach. 4) Code it. 5) Mentally test with the examples.

column1: How do you detect a duplicate in an array efficiently?
column2: Use a Set — traverse the array, if the value is already in the Set it's a duplicate, otherwise add it.

column1: How do you group items (e.g. anagrams) efficiently?
column2: Use a Map, where the key is a normalized "signature" of the item (e.g. sorted string) and the value is the array of items sharing that signature.
